Japan is running out of yttrium. Expect chip prices to rise more.

Open thread • Replies: 7 • Updated: 2026-10-22 05:25 UTC

OP

>Japan is months from running out of supplies of yttrium, a critical metal, and has asked the US to push China to ease rare earth export controls that threaten severe disruption to the global automotive, defence and chip industries.
>Tokyo made the entreaty to the US government and American blue-chip companies, according to people familiar with the matter in Washington and Tokyo.
>Washington has urged China in recent months to increase the flow of rare earths, including yttrium — a heat-resistant metal crucial to manufacturing vehicles, jet engines and semiconductors — to the US and its allies. US defence supply chains rely on components made in Japan that contain yttrium.
>Unless Beijing changes tack or western allies find substitutes or additional stockpiles, shortages could emerge as early as the end of this year, Japanese government officials and trading house executives said.
>“We’re in a serious situation to keep supplying downstream industries,” said a Japanese government official. “Stockpiles are decreasing and rare earth saving efforts have a limit.”
>Yttrium oxide prices outside China have skyrocketed to $1,150 per kilogramme, a 179-fold increase versus two years ago, compared with $9 per kilogramme in China, according to price assessments by Argus.
>The US has complained that China is not fulfilling its pledge to ease rare earth controls under the trade truce the two sides reached last October. After Trump met Xi in Beijing in May, China reiterated that pledge to “address US concerns regarding supply chain shortages related to rare earths...including yttrium”.
>A senior US official told the FT last month that China was fulfilling two-thirds of its rare earth commitments to the US, and was only allowing Japan to procure the bare minimum of its needs.
